title: Rigid Body Motion: Frames, Screws, Twists, And Wrenches
notes: Open by tying the lecture to the assigned notebook and source span: printed pages 19-80 and PDF pages 37-98. The central question is not how to draw a moving body, but how to describe its motion so measurements survive changes of coordinates. Tell students that every object today has two lives: a geometric meaning and a matrix representation.

title: Chapter Map
notes: Use this map to reduce the apparent alphabet soup. The chapter starts with rigid transformations, narrows to rotations in SO(3), then returns to full poses in SE(3). From there the derivative objects appear: twists for velocities and wrenches for forces. The final invariant, power, is the checkpoint that the dual rules are consistent.

title: Rigid Motion Keeps The Body Rigid
notes: Emphasize that a rigid body motion is recognized by what it refuses to change. Pairwise distances and angles in the body remain fixed even while every coordinate listed by an observer may change. This distinction prepares students for why frames are state variables rather than merely labels on a drawing.

title: Rigid Body Transformation
notes: Introduce the familiar formula p_s equals R p_b plus q as a coordinate statement, not as the definition of rigidity. The rotation tells how the body axes are seen in the space frame, while q gives the origin offset. Ask the room to identify which part can change a distance and which part cannot.

title: Frames Are State Variables
notes: The frame lab image should be read as an experiment: the same body-attached coordinates are inspected from different frames. The invariant is the geometry of the marked points; the variable is the table of numbers. This is the conceptual bridge from elementary vector geometry to Lie group kinematics.

title: SO(3): Rotations As A Group
notes: State the two algebraic tests for a rotation matrix and make students connect each test to a geometric meaning. Orthogonality preserves dot products, and determinant one keeps handedness. The multiplication rule is the first reminder that rotations form a group, not just a convenient file format for orientations.

title: Rotation Invariants
notes: This slide slows down the checks that are easy to treat as bookkeeping. Lengths, angles, cross products, and orientation have recognizable algebraic signatures under R. The determinant and orthogonality residuals from the notebook are small because the computation produced an element that behaves like a genuine rotation.

title: Exponential Coordinates For Rotation
notes: Present exponential coordinates as a compact local description: an axis and an angle combined into one vector. The hat map is the bridge from vectors to skew matrices. The important teaching point is that the exponential map turns an infinitesimal generator into a finite rotation while respecting the group structure locally.

title: Local Coordinates Are Fragile
notes: Warn students that minimal coordinates are useful but not neutral. Near special angles, charts can become ambiguous or ill-conditioned, and composition is not simple vector addition. The purpose of this warning is not to discourage exponential coordinates, but to keep the geometric object separate from a particular parameter chart.

title: Homogeneous Transforms And SE(3)
notes: Return to full rigid motion with the block matrix T. The upper-left block rotates, the upper-right block translates, and the bottom row makes affine transformations act linearly on homogeneous coordinates. Stress that SE(3) packages pose into a group element, so inverse and composition have geometric meanings.

title: Composition Order Matters
notes: Use the two routes to make noncommutativity visible. Rotate then translate is usually not the same pose as translate then rotate, even if the same symbols appear. This is the first place where students should stop reading products left to right as ordinary scalar multiplication and start reading them as frame-sensitive actions.

title: Screw Motion
notes: The screw motion explorer condenses Chasles-style intuition: a general rigid displacement can be seen as rotation about an axis together with translation along that axis. Have students inspect the pitch, the helical trace, and the axis label. This visual prepares the derivative version, where twists encode instantaneous screw motion.

title: Twists
notes: Define a twist as the velocity object for a rigid body. The angular part records instantaneous rotation, while the linear part records the velocity of the chosen reference point. The same physical motion will have different six numbers in different frames, so the next slide gives the transformation law rather than a new concept.

title: Adjoint Frame Changes
notes: The adjoint is the rule for moving twist coordinates between frames. Point out the cross-product block: translation changes the linear velocity part because a rotating body gives different point velocities at different origins. The adjoint is therefore not decorative; it is exactly the correction needed when the observer frame moves.

title: Worked Invariant Check
notes: Walk through the saved computation as a compact unit test for the chapter. A twist is pushed through the adjoint, a wrench is pushed through the inverse-transpose rule, and the scalar power pairing is unchanged. The zero power-invariance error is the numerical witness that the two transformation laws match.

title: Wrenches And The Coadjoint Rule
notes: Use the duality figure to distinguish forces from velocities without separating them completely. A wrench pairs with a twist to produce instantaneous power. Because twists move by the adjoint, wrenches must move by the coadjoint rule so the pairing does not depend on which frame was used for the calculation.

title: Inspection Lab And Takeaways
notes: Close by assigning the lab as an inspection task rather than a routine computation. Students should move one twist through three frames, transform the matching wrench correctly, and check which quantities change. The takeaways are the deck's spine: rigid geometry is invariant, coordinates are frame-dependent, and power is the dual consistency test.
